elo-rating.definition: A scoring system commonly used in competitive games like chess: after each match, both players' scores are adjusted based on the gap between the actual result and their pre-match expected win probability: beating a stronger opponent earns more points than beating a weaker one.
elo-rating.application: CodePulse treats the "user" and the "problem" as two competing sides (a correct or incorrect answer counts as one "match") to dynamically adjust the difficulty of the next problem and compute the user's skill rating.

k-factor.definition: The coefficient in the ELO Rating formula that controls how many points a single match can shift; a larger K means a single result has a bigger impact on the score.
k-factor.application: CodePulse decays the K-factor based on how many times the same problem has been attempted (repeated attempts on the same problem get a smaller K), so users can't keep inflating their rating by grinding the same question, keeping the score closer to true ability.

cfg.definition: A graph representation of a program's execution paths: each node represents a block of code, and edges represent possible execution order, such as if/else branches or loop jumps.
cfg.application: When the Playground can't recognize which standard algorithm a user's code corresponds to, it falls back to showing the CFG / call graph, so learners can still see the code's execution path and function-call relationships, just with a lower level of visual abstraction.

ast.definition: The tree structure a compiler or interpreter produces after parsing source code, where each node represents a syntactic element (a loop, a conditional, a function call): the first step in analyzing program structure.
ast.application: The Playground first parses a user's submitted Python code into an AST, which lets it statically derive the control flow graph (CFG) without actually executing the code, forming the basis for later dynamic tracing and visualization.

cosine-similarity.definition: A measure of how similar the direction of two vectors is, ranging from -1 to 1: the closer to 1, the more semantically similar the two are; commonly used to compare code or text after being converted into vectors.
cosine-similarity.application: CodePulse converts a user's code into a semantic vector and compares it against a prebuilt library of standard-algorithm vectors via cosine similarity; a similarity above the threshold (0.80) triggers the corresponding Level 1 semantic animation. The ABSA Pipeline converts each Aspect Term into a semantic vector and compares it against the seed-word vectors of six categories via cosine similarity; the category with the highest similarity becomes the term's assigned category, replacing manual sentence-by-sentence classification.

normalized-gain.definition: A learning-outcome metric common in education research, measuring the "actual improvement" from pre-test to post-test as a fraction of the "maximum possible improvement": the closer to 1, the closer the gain is to a perfect score.
normalized-gain.application: CodePulse's user study used Normalized Gain to measure the change in test scores before and after using the platform; both the university and high-school groups trended positive but did not reach statistical significance, suggesting learning gains were limited but directionally correct given the short session length.

ckip.definition: A Chinese NLP toolkit developed by Academia Sinica's CKIP Lab that performs Chinese word segmentation and part-of-speech (POS) tagging, identifying whether each word is a noun, verb, or another part of speech.
ckip.application: This project uses CKIP (bert-base-chinese) to segment user-feedback sentences and tag their parts of speech, merging adjacent nouns into Aspect Term candidates and keeping stative verbs as Opinion Term candidates.

stanza.definition: A multilingual NLP toolkit from Stanford University, used here for dependency parsing: identifying the grammatical relationships between words in a sentence, such as which word is whose subject or modifier.
stanza.application: Stanza is used to find dependency relations between Aspect Terms and Opinion Terms (e.g., the nsubj subject relation, the amod adjectival-modifier relation) to correctly pair words like "animation" and "smooth" together.

distilbert.definition: A lightweight version of BERT with fewer parameters and faster inference, while retaining most of its language-understanding ability; commonly used for text classification tasks.
distilbert.application: In the final step of the rule-based pipeline, DistilBERT (multilingual version) determines whether an Opinion Term is positive or negative, producing the final polarity label for the Aspect-Opinion pair.

zero-shot.definition: A setting where a model performs a new task directly using only the knowledge learned during pretraining, without additional task-specific training or examples.
zero-shot.application: In Track B, Gemini is given no labeled examples from this dataset: it reads the six categories and rules defined directly in the system prompt and produces ABSA quadruplets in the same format as the rule-based pipeline in a single pass.

partial-f1.definition: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, used to evaluate overall performance on classification/extraction tasks; "Partial" means a looser matching standard is used (counted correct if the text overlaps or is semantically close), rather than requiring an exact character-for-character match.
partial-f1.application: Partial F1 is used to evaluate extraction quality at four levels (Aspect, Opinion, Pair, and Quadruplet), serving as the head-to-head comparison metric between Track A (rule-based) and Track B (Gemini).

agglomerative-clustering.definition: A bottom-up clustering algorithm: each data point starts as its own cluster, and the two closest clusters are repeatedly merged until the desired number of clusters remains.
agglomerative-clustering.application: The project initially tried using Agglomerative Clustering to automatically sort feedback into six categories based on the geometric distance between semantic vectors, but found some categories sat too close together (e.g., UI and Animation differed by only 0.007), blurring the cluster boundaries, so the approach was switched to an Anchor-Guided classification method using manually defined seed words.

b2c.definition: Business-to-Consumer: a trading model where a business sells goods or services directly to end consumers, with no intermediary wholesaler in between.
b2c.application: SilkRoad is a textbook B2C platform: beverage shops list products on the platform, customers order directly, and the entire transaction happens online.

pk-fk.definition: A PK (Primary Key) is the field that uniquely identifies a row in a database table; an FK (Foreign Key) is a field in one table that references another table's primary key, used to establish relationships between tables.
pk-fk.application: SilkRoad uses product_id as an FK to relate the sweetness, ice-level, and size option sub-tables to the product table; the role tables use a 1:1 PK-FK relationship so that ADMIN, CUSTOMER, and VENDOR each extend a shared USER table, simulating inheritance.

crud.definition: An acronym for Create, Read, Update, and Delete: the four basic data operations that nearly every management feature is built from.
crud.application: The Product Management Subsystem (PMS) lets shops perform CRUD on their own products: listing new products, browsing the product list, editing prices or options, and delisting products, though to preserve transaction integrity, "delete" is actually restricted to delisting only; products with existing transaction records can never be truly deleted.

prefetch.definition: Loading a resource before the user actually needs it, for example loading a page as soon as the user hovers over its link. Since the request might go to waste, this is generally only suitable for Safe methods that produce no side effects.
prefetch.application: The HTTP Methods note uses Prefetch to explain why only Safe methods like GET can be safely prefetched by the browser: calling a non-Safe method ahead of time could trigger an unintended change, such as an accidental delete or charge.

safe.definition: An HTTP method property: calling it does not change the state of any Resource on the server. It's a pure read with no side effects beyond logging.
safe.application: The HTTP Methods note uses Safe to determine which methods can be cached by intermediaries like a Proxy or CDN, and even prefetched by the browser: only a method guaranteed to have no side effects can safely be called before the user actually triggers it.

idempotent.definition: An HTTP method property: calling it once or many times leaves the Resource in the same final state. That's a separate question from side effects, e.g. a repeated call might return a different status code the second time, even though the resource's final state doesn't change.
idempotent.application: The HTTP Methods note uses idempotency to decide whether a timed-out request can be safely retried: PUT and DELETE are idempotent and safe to retry, while POST usually isn't, since retrying it can create a duplicate record.

proxy.definition: A server placed between the Client and the real Server that forwards and filters requests on the client's behalf, such as the gateway server that manages all outbound connections on a corporate network.
proxy.application: The HTTP Methods note points out that because Safe methods are guaranteed to have no side effects, a Proxy sitting in between can safely cache their responses instead of forwarding every request all the way to the origin server.

cdn.definition: A network that copies and caches data onto nodes physically closer to end users, making reads faster and saving bandwidth, e.g. Cloudflare.
cdn.application: The HTTP Methods note uses CDN as a concrete example of caching Safe methods: because GET-type requests never change data, a CDN can safely store the response and serve it directly to users without hitting the origin server every time.

rails.definition: A full-stack web framework written in Ruby that favors "Convention over Configuration": as long as you follow its file structure and naming conventions, a lot of boilerplate for routing and database operations is generated automatically instead of being configured by hand in every project.
rails.application: The HTTP Methods note uses Rails' RESTful routing as a concrete example of how Rails maps HTTP method semantics (not just CRUD) onto fixed-name controller actions.

rails-restful-routing.definition: With a single `resources :xxx` declaration, Rails auto-generates a standard set of routes following the HTTP-method-plus-path convention, mapping each one to a fixed controller action name (index/show/create/update/destroy), instead of requiring every route to be written by hand.
rails-restful-routing.application: The HTTP Methods note uses this to show that Rails isn't simply mapping HTTP methods onto CRUD; it's leveraging HTTP's own Resource semantics (GET reads, POST creates, PUT fully sets, PATCH partially modifies, DELETE removes) to build a consistent REST API structure.

normalization.definition: A database design technique that splits data into multiple related tables to reduce duplicate storage and update anomalies; the more finely data is split, the more table joins are typically needed at query time, trading some performance for data integrity.
normalization.application: SilkRoad splits sweetness, ice level, and size options into separate sub-tables instead of cramming every combination into the product table, avoiding duplicate storage of the same option combinations and letting shops adjust options without bulk-updating existing data.

er-model.definition: A blueprint for database design that maps out "entities" (like customers and products) and "relationships" (like a customer purchasing a product): a tool for clarifying data structure and business logic before building actual tables.
er-model.application: SilkRoad's design started from an ER Model, first clarifying the relationships between entities like customers, shops, products, and orders, then splitting customizable attributes (sweetness/ice/size) into separate sub-tables before finally converting everything into an actual database schema.

function-overload.definition: Letting the same function name map to different implementations depending on the type or number of arguments passed in; the compiler automatically picks the matching version at the call site.
function-overload.application: The game's character and object classes use function overloading so that a function with the same name can run different logic depending on the calling context (e.g., initialization or collision handling for different object types), without needing a separately named function for every case.

rls.definition: A security mechanism in databases (like PostgreSQL) that sets visibility or write conditions at the level of individual rows, below the table level: different roles querying the same table may see only the rows that match their conditions.
rls.application: The personal website's Supabase tables use RLS so the anonymous role can only read friend creations where is_visible = true; the invite_codes table has no RLS policy open to the anonymous role at all: codes can only be redeemed indirectly through an RPC, preventing them from being queried and leaked directly.

security-definer.definition: A database function execution mode where the function runs with the privileges of its creator rather than its caller, letting lower-privileged callers perform operations they otherwise couldn't, but only within the logic written inside that function.
security-definer.application: The personal website's invite-code redemption and re-editing flows are both written as security definer RPC functions, letting an anonymous user with no table write permissions at all complete the combined "validate invite code + write friend creation" action, while being restricted to only what the function allows, with no ability to write arbitrary data elsewhere.

race-condition.definition: A bug where multiple operations access and modify the same data at the same time, and the result becomes inconsistent or unexpected depending on execution order; this is common when multiple users or threads read and write the same record simultaneously.
race-condition.application: If two friends submit the same invite code at nearly the same instant, a naive frontend flow of "check if the code is used, then write" could let both pass the check and redeem the code twice. The personal website uses the database's FOR UPDATE to lock the row, ensuring the "check + mark used + write creation" sequence can't be interrupted by another concurrent request. RxJS runs into a different shape of the same problem: when the same action fires repeatedly and sends out several async requests, not flattening them with the right operator can let an older request come back after a newer one, leaving the screen showing a stale result.

intersection-observer.definition: A built-in browser API for detecting whether an element has entered (or left) a given viewport, without manually computing element coordinates inside a scroll handler.
intersection-observer.application: The 3D creature cards on the friends' creation wall use IntersectionObserver to detect whether a card has scrolled into view: only then does it mount a live-rendered Three.js scene, unmounting back to a static placeholder once it scrolls out, so too many WebGL contexts never exist at once and drag down performance.

instancing.definition: A 3D-rendering technique that merges a large number of shapes that share geometry (differing only in position or color) into a single draw call, instead of issuing one draw call per object; it dramatically cuts the rendering overhead of large numbers of repeated geometries.
instancing.application: The 3D creature-painting feature splits an entire creature into hundreds of cubes and merges them into a single instanced render using React Three Fiber's <Instances>; since limit only allocates the buffer size at mount time and doesn't react to later changes, it must be given a sufficiently large fixed upper bound while range dynamically controls how many are actually shown; otherwise, a change in cube count can exceed buffer capacity and fail to render.

visual-analytics.definition: A research field combining interactive visualization with analytical reasoning: letting users manipulate a visual representation of data while reasoning about it, rather than just reading a pre-computed static report; the core concern is whether a visualization actually helps users make better judgments, not just whether it looks good.
visual-analytics.application: CodePulse turns algorithm execution into an interactive animation rather than a plain-text explanation, but the pre/post-test study revealed that "a well-designed interface" and "users genuinely learning more" are two things that need to be verified separately. That gap is exactly why I want to pursue graduate study in Information Visualization / Human-Computer Interaction, to learn more rigorous user-research methods.

interactive-data-exploration.definition: Letting users explore data or a program's execution by directly manipulating it (filtering, drilling down, tracing) rather than passively receiving a pre-packaged conclusion; the exploration path itself is part of understanding the problem.
interactive-data-exploration.application: CodePulse's Playground lets users submit arbitrary code and dynamically traces its execution so users can explore variable changes and function-call relationships themselves, instead of only watching a fixed example animation; this website's own search and category filters on the Projects and Knowledge pages follow the same "let users find their own path" design.

information-visualization.definition: Converting abstract data (numbers, program structure, text statistics) into graphical representations, so people can grasp structure and patterns through visual perception instead of reading line by line.
information-visualization.application: CodePulse renders a program's control flow as a CFG / call graph; the ABSA Pipeline renders user-feedback sentiment results as a word cloud. Both convert processed abstract data into a graphical form whose patterns are visible at a glance.

human-computer-interaction.definition: The field studying how people interact with computer systems, covering usability evaluation and user-research methodology: concerned with rigorously verifying whether a system is actually good to use, rather than relying on intuition.
human-computer-interaction.application: CodePulse's user study recruited two groups (university and high-school students) for a pre/post-test, using Normalized Gain to measure the change in test scores before and after using the platform. This was my first hands-on experience with a common HCI user-research method, and it showed me that "users reporting more confidence" and "a statistically significant test-score improvement" are two pieces of evidence that can't substitute for each other.

thematic-coding.definition: In qualitative research, a code is a label a researcher attaches to a segment of data (an interview transcript, a screenshot) to capture something noteworthy about it; codes that share similar meaning are then grouped and abstracted into a higher-level, more abstract theme. "Tagging" and "coding" are the same act, not two sequential steps where tags get sorted into codes afterward.
thematic-coding.application: In the SnapPI study, the first author coded 21 participants' interview transcripts and returned Snap screenshots, tagging meaning units such as "quantifying feelings that are hard to put into words" or "sharing different stickers depending on friend type"; the team then met regularly to group related codes, converging on 9 codes and 3 core themes.

reflexive-thematic-analysis.definition: A qualitative analysis approach from Braun & Clarke: codes and themes are meaning the researcher subjectively constructs through interpretation, so a different team analyzing the same data may reach different results. That's a natural expression of subjectivity, not an error. Team discussion aims to deepen interpretation, not to compute inter-rater reliability across independent coders the way some other approaches do.
reflexive-thematic-analysis.application: The SnapPI study used reflexive thematic analysis: the first author did the initial coding, and the research team met regularly to revise and consolidate themes, a discussion aimed at deepening interpretation, not at verifying agreement between multiple coders.

natural-language-processing.definition: The research field concerned with having computers understand, analyze, and generate human language (common tasks include word segmentation, part-of-speech tagging, dependency parsing, and sentiment analysis), essentially turning unstructured text into structured information a program can process.
natural-language-processing.application: The ABSA Pipeline compared a rule-based approach (CKIP segmentation + Stanza dependency parsing + DistilBERT sentiment classification) against Gemini Zero-Shot, extracting sentiment quadruplets from user feedback and comparing their Partial F1 scores. It was my first time designing and evaluating a full NLP pipeline end to end.

knowledge-graph.definition: Organizing concepts as nodes and the relationships between them as edges into an interconnected, queryable network of knowledge, so that knowledge isn't just a set of isolated records but something that can cross-reference itself and support reasoning and exploration.
knowledge-graph.application: This website's Knowledge section is itself a small hands-on attempt at this: each technical concept is a node, nodes are connected by prerequisite/related/applies_to/contrasts_with relationships, and each node links back to the projects and articles that reference it. It's still small in scale and manually curated (there's no automated entity/relation extraction or graph visualization yet), but it's my first hands-on implementation of this specific interest.

social-computing.definition: The study of how people interact, share, and present themselves through computer systems and social platforms; the focus isn't just whether a system is usable, but how it both shapes and is shaped by interpersonal interaction, social norms, and context.
social-computing.application: In my SnapPI paper notes, personal data stickers on Snapchat's ephemeral stories lowered the social burden of sharing data and sparked deeper conversations. That showed me information visualization doesn't only serve understanding data, it can also serve communication and self-presentation between people. That's a direction I want to pursue further in graduate research: designing interactive visualization not just as a teaching or analysis tool, but as a medium for communication within social contexts.

interactive-systems.definition: Systems built around a continuous feedback loop between user and system: the user acts, the system responds in real time, and the user adjusts the next action accordingly, rather than the system batch-processing data once and handing back a final result. The design question is whether that loop is fast and legible enough that the user feels like they're operating the system, not waiting on it.
interactive-systems.application: CodePulse's algorithm playground is itself an interactive system: a user submits code, the system renders its execution as a step-by-step animation in real time, and the user adjusts the code and resubmits based on what they see. The platform's value rests on how tight and legible that action-and-feedback loop is, not just on how polished the animation looks.

human-centered-computing.definition: A research approach that starts system design from human needs, capabilities, and values. It's a superordinate concept shared by HCI, social computing, and user-centered design, not a separate research direction alongside them, but the common stance underneath those sub-fields: ask what a technology means for people first, then decide what to build.
human-centered-computing.application: CodePulse's frontend interaction design, user research, A/B crossover study, and pre/post testing look like separate methods on the surface, but they're all answering the same HCC-shaped question underneath: does this design actually help a person.

learning-confidence.definition: A participant's subjective belief about whether they can learn or complete a given learning task, answering "do I believe I can learn this?" It's a psychological construct, not a measurement method in itself.
learning-confidence.application: In CodePulse's pre/post survey, participants rated their confidence in being able to learn harder algorithms going forward, and that confidence rose significantly after using the platform (p < 0.001). A rise in confidence, however, is not the same as a significant gain in test scores (see Normalized Gain); the two are separate pieces of evidence that need to be verified independently.

self-reported-confidence.definition: A measurement method where participants rate their own confidence level on a scale. It's an operationalized measurement technique, not an independent psychological construct, and is commonly used to quantify beliefs like learning confidence.
self-reported-confidence.application: CodePulse's pre/post survey used a rating scale to have participants self-report their confidence in learning algorithms; this self-report method is what makes it possible to turn the change in learning confidence into a comparable number.

self-perceived-learning-effectiveness.definition: A participant's own subjective judgment of how well they learned, answering "do I feel like I learned better?" This is a different layer of evidence from objective learning outcomes measured by test scores, and the two can point in the same direction or diverge.
self-perceived-learning-effectiveness.application: CodePulse's survey asked participants whether, compared to traditional textbooks and slides, they felt CodePulse made the material more intuitive and easier to understand. That kind of answer is self-perceived learning effectiveness, a separate thing from the positive-but-not-significant Normalized Gain shown in test scores.

retrospective-pre-post.definition: A pre/post design where participants answer both a "before" and an "after" self-report item at the same single point in time, usually right after an intervention, rather than being measured once before and once after. Unlike a true pre-post measured on two separate occasions, the "before" rating is actually a recollection made after the fact.
retrospective-pre-post.application: CodePulse's survey items "Before using it, I found algorithms very intimidating" and "After using it, I feel confident I can learn harder algorithms" were both answered together right after the platform session, making this a retrospective pre-post. Treating those two scores as if they came from two separately-administered measurements, when comparing the change in confidence, needs to account for the limits this design carries.

response-shift-bias.definition: When a participant recalls and rates a "before" state after the fact, that rating tends to get colored by how they currently feel, common in retrospective pre-post designs. It isn't participants deliberately misreporting, the recollection itself gets recalibrated by their present cognitive or emotional state.
response-shift-bias.application: CodePulse's survey asked participants, after using the platform, to recall and rate how intimidating they'd found algorithms before. That recollection was likely already colored by the positive experience of using the platform, which could understate the "before" score and inflate the confidence change computed from the pre/post pair.

rxjs.definition: A reactive programming library for JavaScript built around the Observable: async events (user interactions, HTTP responses, timers) are wrapped as streams that emit values over time, and operators compose and transform those streams instead of scattering callbacks or ad hoc async/await logic.
rxjs.application: In the Angular codebase from my internship at Sun Bird Software, async events and API calls ran heavily through RxJS: user interactions and HTTP responses were both Observables, and operators like concatMap, switchMap, mergeMap, and exhaustMap decided what should happen when the same action fired again, instead of hand-rolling flags or timers to manage it.

concat-map.definition: An RxJS flattening operator: when a new inner Observable arrives, it's queued, and only starts once the previous inner Observable completes, so processing order always matches trigger order.
concat-map.application: In the Angular codebase from my internship at Sun Bird Software, concatMap was used for async operations where execution order had to be guaranteed, such as a sequence of requests that had to be sent in order, to keep parallel processing from scrambling that order.

switch-map.definition: An RxJS flattening operator: when a new inner Observable arrives, it immediately cancels whatever inner Observable was still in flight, keeping only the result of the most recent trigger.
switch-map.application: In the Angular codebase from my internship at Sun Bird Software, switchMap was used for search boxes and filters, situations where a user's next action supersedes their previous intent, so the screen only ever shows the result of the latest action instead of getting overwritten by a stale response.

merge-map.definition: An RxJS flattening operator: when a new inner Observable arrives, it runs alongside any still-pending inner Observables in parallel, without cancelling or waiting on each other, with results coming back in whatever order they finish.
merge-map.application: In the Angular codebase from my internship at Sun Bird Software, mergeMap was used for async operations that were independent of each other with no ordering requirement, letting multiple requests run at once instead of queuing.

exhaust-map.definition: An RxJS flattening operator: when a new inner Observable arrives, if the previous inner Observable hasn't completed yet, the new trigger is dropped outright, and only the next trigger after the current one finishes gets accepted. It's the mirror of switchMap: switchMap lets the new one override the old, exhaustMap lets whatever's already running finish and ignores the new one.
exhaust-map.application: In the Angular codebase from my internship at Sun Bird Software, exhaustMap was used for submit buttons and similar cases where an in-flight operation shouldn't be interrupted or duplicated, preventing a form from being submitted twice if a user clicked again before the first request came back.

debounce-time.definition: An RxJS operator that only lets the latest value through once a specified amount of time has passed with no new events, used to throttle events that fire rapidly in a short span (like typing). It's a different layer of problem from what concatMap, switchMap, and mergeMap deal with, how to flatten a nested Observable.
debounce-time.application: In the Angular codebase from my internship at Sun Bird Software, debounceTime was paired with switchMap to handle search-box input: debounceTime filtered out the intermediate keystrokes and only let a request fire once the user paused for a moment, and switchMap then made sure only the latest request's result got used.

map.definition: An RxJS operator that transforms each value in the stream into a new value, one to one, without changing how many values there are.

filter.definition: An RxJS operator that only lets values matching a condition through, dropping the rest without changing the ones that pass.

tap.definition: An RxJS operator that doesn't change the data itself, it just runs a side effect (like logging or debugging) partway through the stream, commonly used to observe the current value without affecting it.

distinct-until-changed.definition: An RxJS operator that skips a new value if it's the same as the previous one, only letting a value through when it actually changes, to avoid triggering downstream logic again for a repeated value.

catch-error.definition: An RxJS operator that catches an error in the stream and swaps in a new Observable to keep going, so the stream doesn't just die on a single error.

retry.definition: An RxJS operator that automatically resubscribes to the original Observable a set number of times when the stream errors out, commonly used for transient network failures.

fork-join.definition: An RxJS combination operator that waits for every Observable passed in to complete, then emits each one's final value at once, commonly used when several API calls need to finish before continuing.

take-one.definition: An RxJS operator that takes only the first value from the stream and then unsubscribes automatically, good for data that only needs to be read once.

take-until.definition: An RxJS operator that keeps subscribing until another Observable it's given emits a value, then unsubscribes automatically, often paired with a Subject that emits on component destroy to clean up subscriptions in one place.

ngrx.definition: A state-management library implementing the Redux pattern for the Angular ecosystem. The core idea is centralizing app state in a single Store: an Action declares that an event happened, a Reducer computes the new state, an Effect handles side effects (like API calls), and a Selector reads state, letting components share data without talking to each other directly.
ngrx.application: In the Angular codebase from my internship at Sun Bird Software, several components with no direct parent-child relationship needed to share and stay in sync on the same data (user info, filter state), managed centrally through NgRx's Store instead of each component keeping its own copy in a service, which is prone to falling out of sync.

onpush.definition: An Angular performance optimization: by default, any event triggers a check of the whole component tree for re-rendering; a component set to OnPush only gets re-checked in a handful of cases, most commonly when an incoming @Input is compared with === and found to be a different reference.
onpush.application: In the Angular codebase from my internship at Sun Bird Software, OnPush was paired with NgRx: because a reducer always returns a new object instead of mutating the existing state, an OnPush component can correctly detect that the data actually changed via reference comparison, and only re-render when it needs to.

signal.definition: Angular's built-in reactivity primitive: signal() creates a readable, writable state container, computed() creates a derived value that automatically recomputes when the signals it depends on change, and a template that reads a signal directly re-renders whenever the value changes, no Store, no subscribing to an Observable.
signal.application: In the Angular codebase from my internship at Sun Bird Software, state that only mattered inside a single component and didn't need to be shared with components outside its parent-child chain (like whether a form section was expanded or collapsed) was handled with Signal instead of being forced into NgRx's Store for consistency, avoiding unnecessary Action/Reducer boilerplate.
